passage:
Sunday, week one. Usha's phone showed Imran's last message from nine days ago, a photo of his hostel mess dinner. She had not replied either. She felt a small ache and put the phone face down.

Thursday, week three. Usha stopped waiting for him to text first and sent a voice note: "Saw a dog that looks exactly like the one outside your old gate. Hope engineering is not eating you alive 🙂." No question, no "why so silent".

Saturday, week six. Imran answered at midnight with a long message about his new lab partner and a bad exam. They talked for twenty minutes. It was nothing like school, when they met every day, and Usha noticed she no longer expected it to be. She put a call in her diary for the first Sunday of each month and left the rest loose.

qa.q: What did Usha send when she stopped waiting for Imran to text first?
qa.a: She sent a voice note about a dog that looks exactly like the one outside his old gate, with no complaint in it.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she put the phone face down?
qa.a: A quiet sense of loss. The passage says she felt a small ache, and she set the phone down instead of firing off a message.

qa.q: What is worth copying in how Usha handled the distance?
qa.a: She reached out lightly without keeping score, and later set a monthly call, which keeps the friendship going without expecting it to match their school days.

qa.q: How might Imran have taken Usha's voice note after all those silent days?
qa.a: Probably as an easy, warm way back in. With no blame in it, he could reply without feeling guilty, which fits his long midnight reply.

grounding: Two friends in different cities drift apart; Usha feels the quiet loss, reaches out without scorekeeping, and lets the friendship become smaller.

passage:
Sunday, 11 p.m.
Uday posted photos from his hostel's Diwali night in Kharagpur. Fifteen people I don't know, all in kurtas, him in the middle grinning. I liked it and then stared at it way too long.
We used to talk every day in school. Now it's maybe once a month, and it's usually me calling. Tonight I almost typed "nice, glad you've replaced us" and deleted it, because that's not even what I feel. What I feel is that something quiet has gone missing.
So I sent: "Looks fun! Miss our terrace chai. Call sometime this week?" No counting who called last. If he replies in three days, fine. If we end up being once-a-month friends, maybe that's what this is now, and it's still something.
He replied at 11:40: "YES 😄 Wednesday?"
Going to sleep lighter.
— Vishal

qa.q: Where was Uday's hostel Diwali night?
What was Vishal feeling while staring at Uday's photos?
qa.a: A quiet sense of loss with a flash of bitterness; the "replaced us" message came from that, but sadness was the truer feeling.

qa.q: What did Vishal try instead of sulking or cutting Uday off?
qa.a: A warm message suggesting a call, without counting who called last, and a readiness to accept a smaller friendship.

qa.q: How might Uday see Vishal's message?
qa.a: As a happy surprise; his quick "YES" suggests he misses Vishal too, even with a busy new life.

grounding: Shows friends drifting apart across cities, the quiet loss of it, and reaching out without keeping score.

passage:
Two days after her birthday, which Damini had missed, Hafsa opened their chat. The last message was from March.
Hafsa: hey stranger! how's pune treating you?
Damini: hafsa!! 🥺 wait. your birthday. i'm so sorry
Hafsa: it's ok, honestly. i almost sent something sulky
Hafsa: then i realised i just miss you
Damini: i miss you too. work is eating me alive, i'm asleep by 10 most nights
Hafsa: no score keeping, ok? i'll text when i think of you, you reply when you can
Damini: deal. and i'm still calling you on your next birthday, i've set a reminder already
Hafsa: haha ok
Damini: voice notes on sunday mornings? even two minutes?
Hafsa: perfect. two minutes counts
Damini: sending one tomorrow with a pune rain update ☔
Hafsa: 🤍

qa.q: What did Hafsa realise after almost sending something sulky?
qa.a: That the real feeling was missing Damini, a quiet sadness rather than anger.

qa.q: Which choice kept the friendship alive?
qa.a: Hafsa reached out warmly, dropped the score-keeping, and they agreed on short Sunday voice notes that fit Damini's tiring job.

qa.q: How does Damini feel when Hafsa writes first?
qa.a: Guilty about the missed birthday, but relieved and touched that Hafsa isn't angry.

grounding: Illustrates a friendship shrinking with distance and a new job, and choosing to reach out without keeping score instead of sulking.
